extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, history of mathematics, and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Plato's methodological and definitional standards for mathematics as presented in the scholarly discussion (distinctions among name/definition/particular/idea; hypotheses; the two intellectual methods; definitions of geometric primitives; treatment of incommensurables; construction of solids; classical problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold classification of linguistic/ontological levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish name, definition, particular drawn/turned object, and the essential idea (avTov 6 kvkXos / the idea of circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's classification: (1) the name is merely conventional (we could call round 'straight'); (2) the definition is made of parts of speech and lacks real definiteness; (3) the particular (the circle drawn or turned) is perishable and mixed with opposites (e.g., tangent contact); (4) the essential circle (idea) is the one by reference to which the other circles exist and is different from each of them. The passage stresses that particular mathematical drawings are intermediate between imperfect particulars and the single idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses of mathematics (primitive assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians take certain things (odd and even, figures, three kinds of angles, etc.) as hypotheses and treat them as manifest without giving explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who occupy themselves with geometry assume these elements as known and proceed from them to conclusions; they make use of visible figures but think of the absolute counterparts (the absolute square, absolute diameter) rather than the drawn figure. Hypotheses function as starting-points for further argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two intellectual methods (geometrical vs. dialectical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato distinguishes: (a) a method that treats hypotheses as if they were first principles and uses diagrams/images to derive conclusions (geometry/mathematics), and (b) the dialectical method which treats hypotheses as hypotheses and uses them as stepping-stones to reach a non-hypothetical first principle and then descend back in connected steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first method cannot get above its hypotheses; the second 'rises above and puts an end to hypotheses' and reaches first principles without needing sensible images. Without the dialectical method, geometry and other sciences are 'comparable to one dreaming about truth' since they treat hypotheses as immovable truths and cannot account for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of analysis and method of division (Proclus' account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two handed-down methods: (1) analysis — carry the thing sought up to an acknowledged principle; (2) division — successively bipartition genera into species to give a starting-point for demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis (in the philosophical sense) corresponds to Plato's dialectical ascent; division (as in Sophist and Politicus) is useful in non-geometrical contexts. Importance is placed on synthesis following analysis for logical rigour. The passage suggests possible historical confusion between mathematical analysis (reduction) and philosophical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper formation of definitions and true divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and divisions must be appropriate to the subject: e.g., proper division of number is into odd and even; other divisions (myriads vs non-myriads) are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato paid attention to definitions: an even number defined as divisible into two equal parts; other formulations (e.g., using 'scalene'/'isosceles' analogies) may be defective unless terms are properly restricted. The principle is to use genus/species distinctions and true divisions that reflect the nature of the thing defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric primitive definitions should avoid reliance on perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Define geometric primitives (line, straight, point, figure) in terms fitting the subject-matter and not by appeal to vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: line as 'breadthless length'; straight line as 'that of which the middle covers the ends' (leading toward Euclid's 'lies evenly with the points on it'); point criticized as a 'geometrical fiction' by Plato/Aristotle. Plato's suggestion that figure is the limit (extremity) of a solid parallels Euclid's boundary notion. The guidance is to formulate definitions without recourse to sensory descriptions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of circle and sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle: 'that in which the furthest points in all directions are at the same distance from the middle (centre)'; Sphere: equidistant from centre in all directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distance/equidistance to define round objects; these are canonical geometrical definitions in the Platonic tradition (cf. Timaeus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include axioms and preliminary distinctions in mathematical foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and state axioms and preliminary distinctions (e.g., distinction between 'a part' and 'parts'; axioms like 'If equals be added to unequals, the sums differ by the same amount').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's texts contain phrases corresponding to Euclid's preliminary matter; such preliminary axiomatic statements and careful terminological distinctions belong in foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of regular solids from planar faces and triangular decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular solids are constructed by assembling plane faces, with faces built from triangles; triangles decompose into right-angled triangles of two basic kinds (isosceles and scalene), which determine which solids arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato (via Theaetetus) describes the five regular solids: cube faces made of isosceles right triangles, tetrahedron/octahedron/icosahedron depend on the other species of right-angled triangle, dodecahedron requires pentagons and cannot be built from the two elementary right triangles. Historical notes: connections to Pythagorean constructions and pentagram decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorems on geometric means between square and cube numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Between two square numbers there is one mean proportional; between two cube numbers two mean proportionals are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's Timaeus alludes to these theorems (cf. Euclid VIII.11,12). Historically these results relate to the problems like duplication of the cube and mean proportionals appearing earlier (Hippocrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of hypothesis in problem-solving and determination of solvability (Sioptaixo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hypothesis to reduce a problem and thereby determine (give a Sioptaixo) the conditions/limits under which a construction is possible or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Meno passages: Socrates 'by way of hypothesis' reduces the problem of inscribing a given area as a triangle in a given circle to applying a rectangle to the diameter that 'falls short' by a similar figure. This reduction leads to an equation (hyperbola intersecting circle) whose solvability determines possibility. The method is also used to show whether a solution exists (limits such as being no greater than the maximum inscribable triangle). The text emphasizes that the criterion sought is a real determination of possibility/limits, not a mere restatement of special parameter values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of classical unsolvable/special problems and use of conic/auxiliary methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems like inscribing a triangle of given area in a circle or finding two mean proportionals may require conics (hyperbola, intersection of conic and circle) and are not solvable by straightedge-and-compass alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Meno passage reduces the problem to solving a quartic via intersections of conics; historical note that such problems were later solved by conic constructions (Menaechmus) or mechanical methods (ruler manipulations). The passage suggests Plato was aware some geometric problems transcended straight line and circle methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation of integer solutions for x^2 + y^2 = z^2 (Pythagorean formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato (or Pythagorean tradition credited to Plato) is associated with a rule/formula for finding series of square numbers whose sum is a square, e.g., the formula given for producing such triples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific formula is quoted (in the text's notation) for generating square sums; the passage links Platonic/Pythagorean traditions with rules complementary to Pythagoras' rules. This is treated as part of Plato's mathematical material rather than an innovation necessarily beyond his contemporaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness and treatment of incommensurables (irrationals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that lengths/breadths/depths may be incommensurable as well as commensurable; irrational quantities may combine to give rational or irrational sums; awareness of 'golden section' irrationalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato (Laws, Theaetetus) comments on the ignorance of incommensurables and implies familiarity with irrational straight lines such as those arising from division in extreme and mean ratio. The passage suggests theorems about irrational segments (Euclid Book X notions) may predate Plato or be contemporary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mystical/numerological constructs in philosophical-mathematical discourse (Geometrical Number)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonic passages (e.g., the Geometrical Number in the Republic) mix mystical/rhapsodical language with a few mathematical conceptions (cubes, ratios like 4:3 joined to 5) to encode cosmological or pedagogical constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Geometrical Number is treated as mystic rather than strictly mathematical, though commentators (Hultsch, Adam) extract candidate numerical interpretations (e.g., 216 as sum of cubes). The guidance: recognize the rhetorical/mystical framing and the occasional embedding of concrete arithmetical structure (cubes, harmonic ratios).
